title: The Invocation Matrix — Who Can Trigger It

questions.prompt: You author a skill that publishes release notes. It fired on its own once during an unrelated task. You add a switch so that cannot happen again — and now a teammate's slash command no longer does anything. Which single change fixes both?
options: Remove the switch and rely on a stricter description instead
Set user-invocable: false, which hides it from the menu and from the model
Set disable-model-invocation: true and leave user-invocable at its default, so the model can't pick it but /name still works
Set both switches, since the skill must be run by someone and there is no cell for that
questions.explanation: The two failures came from treating invocation as one flag. disable-model-invocation is the switch that stops the surprise, and user-invocable defaults to true, so /name keeps working — that is cell 2, and it also removes the description from the listing you were paying for. Option B picks the switch that stops the wrong caller: it hides the skill from you and leaves Claude free. Option D produces cell 4, which is neither caller — and there is a cell for exactly what this skill wants, which is the one option A refuses to find.

questions.prompt: You own about fifteen skills you only ever type yourself, and /context shows the Skills row is now the largest fixed cost in your window. Which observation is true?
options: The listing cost is unavoidable — every installed skill's description sits in the window regardless of how it is invoked
Setting disable-model-invocation: true on the manual-only ones removes their descriptions from the model's available-skill context, so they stop costing listing budget
Set user-invocable: false on them instead, since that is the switch that removes them from the listing
Only /context with the skills deleted shows the real cost, so there is nothing to optimise while they are installed
questions.explanation: The docs state that a disable-model-invocation skill has its description removed from Claude's available-skill context — which is why cell 2 is also the cheap cell. Option A states the opposite of that, and it is the belief that makes people assume skills are free. Option C swaps the switches; user-invocable false keeps the skill *in* the listing while hiding it from you, which is exactly backwards for this goal. Option D gives up before measuring.

questions.prompt: Two skills are named deploy — one at .claude/skills/deploy/, one at apps/web/.claude/skills/deploy/. Which is the accurate picture?
options: The second one silently loses; only the first gets a command
Both get a command, and the nested one is invoked as /apps/web:deploy
The nested one shadows the root one and both are invoked as /deploy
The root one must be renamed, because two skills cannot share a command name
questions.explanation: Nested skills that clash with another skill are addressed by prefixing the path relative to the working directory, then the skill's own name — which is why the colon form looks unusual and is not a typo. Option A invents a silent shadowing rule that would make monorepos unusable. Option C reverses it: the root one is the plain /deploy, not the other way round. Option D is wrong because the mechanism exists precisely so that neither has to be renamed.
